lower_back.md.title: Lower Back
lower_back.md.content:
# Lower Back

Lumbar support and lower back strain exercises.

- Sit with hips slightly higher than knees and maintain neutral spine.
- Use a cushion or lumbar roll if the chair lacks proper support.
- Add standing breaks and gentle lumbar mobility exercises throughout the day.

neck.md.title: Neck Relief
neck.md.content:
# Neck Relief

Cervical stretch and neck pain relief guidance.

- Adjust monitor height so the top of the screen is at eye level.
- Use a supportive chair with lumbar support and avoid forward head posture.
- Perform gentle neck rotations and chin tucks periodically.

wrist.md.title: Wrist Setup
wrist.md.content:
# Wrist Setup

Advice for wrist pain and ulnar soreness when typing.

- Use a neutral wrist posture when typing.
- Keep the keyboard close and at elbow height.
- Take frequent short breaks and perform wrist stretches.

cervical_neck_shoulder.md.title: Fixing Cervical Neck and Shoulder Tightness
cervical_neck_shoulder.md.content:
# Fixing Cervical Neck and Shoulder Tightness

A stiff neck and tight shoulder muscles often result from looking down at a laptop for extended periods. This cervical fatigue quickly leads to a sore neck and general shoulder pain. 

Raise your monitor so the top third of the screen is at eye level. When your screen is too low, your neck carries the heavy weight of your head, leaving your cervical spine tired, tight, and stiff by the end of the day.

lower_back_lumbar.md.title: Relieving Lower Back and Lumbar Soreness
lower_back_lumbar.md.content:
# Relieving Lower Back and Lumbar Soreness

If you experience lower back pain or lumbar soreness after long hours at your desk, your chair might be the problem. A stiff or tight lower back usually means a lack of proper lumbar support. 

To prevent a sore back, ensure your chair supports the natural curve of your spine. Taking breaks to stand and stretch will reduce fatigue and stop the dull ache associated with poor sitting habits.

wrist_ulnar_hand.md.title: Wrist, Hand, and Ulnar Pain Relief
wrist_ulnar_hand.md.content:
# Wrist, Hand, and Ulnar Pain Relief

Typing on a flat keyboard without ergonomic support often causes wrist fatigue and hand soreness. Ulnar deviation—bending your wrist outward toward your pinky—can cause sharp pain or a persistent ache that travels up to the elbow. 

To fix this, keep your wrist perfectly neutral and let your elbow rest comfortably at a 90-degree angle. Stretching your hand regularly will relieve a tired wrist and reduce ulnar tightness.

ankle_calf_foot.md.title: Reducing Ankle, Calf, and Foot Discomfort
ankle_calf_foot.md.content:
# Reducing Ankle, Calf, and Foot Discomfort

Foot ache, calf tightness, and ankle stiffness often increase when your feet do not rest flat on the floor. Unsupported legs can also lead to lower limb fatigue and restless discomfort during work.

Use a footrest if needed, keep both feet grounded, and perform ankle pumps during the day. Small mobility drills for calves and ankles improve comfort and reduce lower leg tension.

break_microstretch_routine.md.title: Microbreak and Stretch Routine for Desk Fatigue
break_microstretch_routine.md.content:
# Microbreak and Stretch Routine for Desk Fatigue

Continuous focus without breaks increases total muscular fatigue and makes pain signals stronger over time. Small aches in the neck, back, wrists, and eyes often come from static load, not one single movement.

Take a 2 to 3 minute microbreak each hour for breathing, shoulder rolls, and light stretching. Consistent short resets reduce cumulative tension better than waiting for severe discomfort.

elbow_forearm_tendon.md.title: Managing Elbow and Forearm Tendon Pain
elbow_forearm_tendon.md.content:
# Managing Elbow and Forearm Tendon Pain

Forearm tightness and elbow pain can come from repetitive typing, gripping a mouse too hard, or unsupported wrists. Over time this strain can feel like tendon irritation near the inner or outer elbow.

Keep your forearms supported, reduce mouse grip force, and alternate high repetition tasks when possible. Gentle wrist flexor and extensor stretches plus light movement breaks can calm tendon stress and reduce forearm soreness.

eye_strain_headache.md.title: Reducing Eye Strain and Tension Headaches
eye_strain_headache.md.content:
# Reducing Eye Strain and Tension Headaches

Eye strain, dry eyes, and screen headaches often appear after staring at bright monitors without breaks. If your eyes feel tired, blurry, or heavy, your visual system is working too hard and your neck may also tighten.

Use the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Lower glare, increase text size, and keep the monitor about an arm length away to reduce visual fatigue and headache pressure.

hip_flexor_glute.md.title: Relieving Hip Flexor and Glute Fatigue
hip_flexor_glute.md.content:
# Relieving Hip Flexor and Glute Fatigue

Long desk sessions shorten your hip flexors and reduce glute activation, which can cause hip tightness, buttock soreness, and lower body fatigue. You may notice discomfort when standing up after sitting too long.

Set a timer to stand every 30 to 45 minutes, then do a brief hip flexor stretch and 10 bodyweight glute squeezes. This resets pelvic position, improves circulation, and lowers the ache from prolonged sitting.

jaw_tmj_tension.md.title: Releasing Jaw and TMJ Workstation Tension
jaw_tmj_tension.md.content:
# Releasing Jaw and TMJ Workstation Tension

Stress and intense focus can make you clench your jaw without noticing, which may trigger TMJ pain, temple pressure, and neck tension. This pattern often appears during long, high concentration computer tasks.

Keep your tongue lightly on the roof of your mouth, lips closed, and teeth slightly apart to relax the jaw. Add slow breathing and a short jaw release routine to reduce clenching and facial muscle fatigue.

keyboard_split_tenting.md.title: Preventing Keyboard Overreach and Wrist Deviation
keyboard_split_tenting.md.content:
# Preventing Keyboard Overreach and Wrist Deviation

A straight, wide keyboard can force shoulder abduction and ulnar deviation, causing wrist pain, forearm fatigue, and shoulder tension. Reaching too far also increases neck and upper back strain.

Center your keyboard to your torso, keep elbows close, and angle input devices to maintain neutral wrists. A split keyboard with mild tenting can reduce deviation and improve comfort for heavy typing workloads.

knee_leg_circulation.md.title: Improving Knee Comfort and Leg Circulation
knee_leg_circulation.md.content:
# Improving Knee Comfort and Leg Circulation

Knee stiffness and heavy legs are common when your chair height is off or you stay still for hours. Poor circulation can create numbness, tingling, or a cramped feeling around the knees and calves.

Adjust your chair so knees are near 90 degrees with feet fully supported. Add frequent standing or short walks to restore blood flow and reduce knee pressure from static desk posture.

laptop_mobile_setup.md.title: Correcting Laptop and Mobile Device Posture
laptop_mobile_setup.md.content:
# Correcting Laptop and Mobile Device Posture

Laptop and phone use often drive a forward head posture, rounded shoulders, and wrist compression. This can lead to neck pain, shoulder tightness, and thumb or hand fatigue by the end of the day.

Raise your laptop with a stand, use an external keyboard and mouse, and hold your phone at eye level when possible. Frequent posture resets prevent cumulative strain from portable device habits.

mid_back_thoracic.md.title: Easing Mid Back and Thoracic Tightness
mid_back_thoracic.md.content:
# Easing Mid Back and Thoracic Tightness

A rounded sitting posture can overload the thoracic spine and create a dull ache between your shoulder blades. Mid back stiffness usually builds when your keyboard and monitor pull your body forward for long periods.

Bring your screen closer, sit with your ribs stacked over your hips, and keep your shoulders relaxed instead of shrugged. A short thoracic extension stretch every hour helps reduce mid back pain and restores upright posture.

mouse_grip_clicking.md.title: Fixing Mouse Grip and Clicking Strain
mouse_grip_clicking.md.content:
# Fixing Mouse Grip and Clicking Strain

Click-heavy work can overload your index finger, wrist, and forearm, especially if your mouse is too small or far from your body. This repetitive strain may feel like burning, aching, or sharp pain during long sessions.

Place the mouse close to your keyboard, keep your wrist neutral, and use your whole arm to move the pointer when possible. Lower click force, increase pointer speed, and alternate hands occasionally to reduce overuse.

standing_desk_transition.md.title: Using a Standing Desk Without New Pain
standing_desk_transition.md.content:
# Using a Standing Desk Without New Pain

Switching to standing all day too quickly can create foot pain, low back fatigue, and calf tightness. Even healthy posture changes can overload tissues if the transition is too aggressive.

Start with short standing intervals, such as 15 to 20 minutes each hour, then progress gradually. Keep knees soft, alternate weight between legs, and use supportive footwear to reduce standing related discomfort.
